paragraphs.text: At 8:37 on the morning of August 26, seismographs recorded a magnitude 5.2 shock in the mountains of Nepal, near the border with Tibet. The US Geological Survey first listed it as an earthquake. It was not one.

stat.label: The shock recorded at 08:37, 26 August 2026
How the US Geological Survey first listed it

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 2.jpg

paragraphs.text: This is the valley below it last October. And this is the same valley this October. That grey line running down the mountain was not there a year ago.
What the instruments heard was a piece of mountain falling. A block of ice and rock broke off the north side of Langtang Lirung, a peak of 7,227 metres, and dropped more than a kilometre.

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 4.jpg
File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 6.jpg

paragraphs.text: It became a flood that ran about a hundred kilometres into Nepal. When the search ended on October 5, Nepal counted 1,455 dead and 5,285 still missing.

stat.label: And 5,285 still missing in Nepal, 5 October 2026

paragraphs.text: A preliminary study says the ice had been moving unusually fast for two years, and satellites recorded it. So why did the warning reach phones thirty-eight minutes after the collapse? And why was this the third time in eleven years that this valley was destroyed?

stat.label: From the collapse to the text alerts

ask.text: Could anyone have seen it coming?

paragraphs.text: The ice and rock fell about eight kilometres down a side valley into the Lhende river, on the Tibetan side of the border. On the way it picked up loose rock, mud and water.

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 2.jpg

paragraphs.text: Then the flood turned west, toward the border crossing at Rasuwagadhi, about thirteen kilometres downstream. On the Chinese side stands Gyirong Port, which handled close to a third of Nepal's trade with China, by Chinese figures.

Cameras there filmed the water arriving within minutes. Chinese state television showed it hitting the customs and immigration building. Some experts put its speed at more than a hundred kilometres an hour.

stat.label: The flood's speed, by some experts' estimates

paragraphs.text: After a flood here the year before, the Chinese side had built a new flood wall and dikes and held an evacuation drill. The water went through them in minutes.
China's premier, Li Qiang, was in Gyirong the same day. A makeshift road to the port was finished a week later, and trade moved to the Korala crossing, far to the west.
On the Nepali side it took the customs office and the dry port, with its containers and trucks. More than three hundred vehicles were swept away.

stat.label: Vehicles swept away at Rasuwagadhi

paragraphs.text: From here the river is called the Bhotekoshi. It runs south through a narrow gorge, past Timure, to Syafrubesi, where trekkers start the walk into Langtang.
The road through this gorge was the main truck route to China. The Kathmandu Post wrote that the all-weather route to Kerung was no more.
Then the Trishuli: below the hill town of Dhunche, past Mailung and Betrawati, down to Trishuli and Devighat, about a hundred kilometres from where the ice fell.

And the danger did not end that morning. The debris dammed the river in Tibet, and two lakes formed behind it. Two days later, Chinese authorities warned that one of them, holding about two million cubic metres, could burst. Rescue work in Nepal stopped while it overflowed. It drained over the next two days without a second disaster.

stat.label: Water held by one barrier lake in Tibet, 28 August

paragraphs.text: Bodies were later recovered far downstream, some across the border in India. So who was warned, and when?

ask.text: Who should have sounded the alarm?

paragraphs.text: Nepal does have a flood warning system on this river. It was built for the monsoon: rain that swells a river over hours, watched by gauges upstream.
This flood started above all of them. The stations nearest the border were swept away before they could warn anyone.
A fellow at the Stimson Center, a research institute in Washington, called this stretch of the border a monitoring blind spot. Nothing on either side was watching the ice in real time.

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 2.jpg

paragraphs.text: Officials in Rasuwa called the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology at about nine. Text alerts went out at about 9:15, more than six hundred thousand of them. That was thirty-eight minutes after the collapse.

stat.label: Text alerts sent around 9:15

paragraphs.text: Once it started, the system was fast: almost 680,000 messages went out within a minute. A former environment minister still flagged the delay and called for better communication.

stat.label: Text alerts sent within one minute

paragraphs.text: For Rasuwagadhi and Timure it came far too late. Farther down the river, every minute counted.
In Trishuli, a headteacher named Rajendra Dawadi moved about nine hundred children out of his school. The BBC and the Guardian reported that the flood reached it ten minutes later.
Across the border, Tibetan officials said about twenty minutes passed between the collapse and the surge, and that a warning in that window could have saved lives.

stat.label: From collapse to surge, Tibetan officials said

paragraphs.text: The Kathmandu Post summed it up in its headline: the alert went out thirty-eight minutes after the collapse, and it was not enough.

document.text: Nepal sent its disaster alert 38 minutes after the glacier collapse. It wasn't enough

paragraphs.text: None of this was new to this valley. On April 25, 2015, at 11:56 in the morning, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake shook Nepal, about seventy kilometres west of here.

stat.label: The Gorkha earthquake, 25 April 2015, 11:56

paragraphs.text: On the south side of the same mountain, a hanging block of glacier broke loose. Within minutes, the debris buried almost all of Langtang village.
ICIMOD found that the eight highest villages of the valley were destroyed, not just Langtang.
Langtang was a trekking village, with fifty-five guesthouses. Its people call the valley a beyul, a hidden sacred refuge, and Langtang Lirung its protector.

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 3.jpg

paragraphs.text: The blast of air in front of it flattened buildings that had survived and knocked down a forest of grown trees. Here is the valley from orbit that October.

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 5.jpg

paragraphs.text: Officially 306 people died: at least 175 of about 370 villagers who were there, 82 other Nepalis and 49 foreign trekkers. The villagers say it was closer to five hundred.

stat.label: The villagers' own count of the dead

paragraphs.text: They rebuilt it themselves, about a hundred metres up the valley. This is Langtang last February.
Then, last year, the danger came from the other side of the border. On July 8, 2025, a lake on top of a glacier in Tibet burst, about thirty-six kilometres above Rasuwagadhi.
It sat at 5,150 metres and had grown quickly from December to June. The Kathmandu Post called it previously unnoticed. After it burst, it still covered 0.61 square kilometres.

stat.label: The lake before it burst, at 5,150 metres

paragraphs.text: The flood took the Friendship Bridge at Rasuwagadhi, wrecked the dry port and hit hydropower plants down the river. Police counted nine dead and nineteen missing.
A disaster specialist at ICIMOD, the regional mountain research centre, told the paper: "The acceleration of these types of events is completely unprecedented."

shots.on_screen_text: Glaciers on the Tibetan side of the Himalaya, ISS, May 2026

document.text: The acceleration of these types of events is completely unprecedented in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region.
document.source: Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD, to the Kathmandu Post, 2025

paragraphs.text: The road along the river was still being repaired when this summer's flood came down it. So what exactly broke this time, and why?
This is the source, around five thousand two hundred metres up on the north face. A year before. And after: a scar where the ice and rock used to be.

How much fell is still argued. The geologist Ranjan Kumar Dahal gives a conservative satellite estimate of twenty-five million cubic metres. Others put it at forty, a hundred, or a hundred and forty-two million.

chart.title: How much fell? Estimates, million m³
chart.source: Ranjan Kumar Dahal, Tribhuvan University, via OnlineKhabar, Sep 2, 2026; HiRISK

paragraphs.text: His team describes the main avalanche as about 1.3 kilometres long and sixty to seventy metres thick. Two days later, a smaller slide fell from the same place.

stat.label: Thickness of the main avalanche, about 1.3 km long
stat.source: Ranjan Kumar Dahal, Tribhuvan University, via OnlineKhabar, Sep 2, 2026

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 4.jpg
File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 6.jpg

paragraphs.text: Even the smallest figure, Dahal says, is about ten times the volume of the Great Pyramid.

stat.label: The Great Pyramid's volume, in the smallest estimate
stat.source: Ranjan Kumar Dahal, Tribhuvan University, via OnlineKhabar, Sep 2, 2026

paragraphs.text: The Chamoli disaster in northern India in 2021, which left about two hundred people dead or missing, was around twenty-seven million cubic metres.

Why did it fall? A preliminary study from the Chinese Academy of Sciences used Sentinel-2 images and found that the glacier's upper and middle parts had been moving relatively fast for the past two years.
It found no rain trigger: 8.8 millimetres in the three days before. Winter had been 0.38 degrees above average, summer 0.58.

stat.label: Rain in the 72 hours before: not the trigger
stat.source: Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research (CAS), preliminary, via OnlineKhabar, Sep 3, 2026

paragraphs.text: The same study found something else. Seismic instruments picked up unusual signals that morning, at about 6:04, 6:50 and again from 8:15. Some matched dust and small slides that local people reported. The researchers say that is not enough to call them a warning.

chart.title: Unusual signals, morning of 26 August
chart.source: Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research (CAS), preliminary, via OnlineKhabar, Sep 3, 2026

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 4.jpg

paragraphs.text: The researchers list several processes working together, from freezing and thawing inside the rock to damage left by the 2015 earthquake.

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa 6.jpg

paragraphs.text: The glaciers here have been shrinking for decades. A 2026 study found that Langtang's glaciers retreated one and a half times faster after 2000 than before it.

stat.label: Faster retreat of Langtang glaciers, 2000-2023 against 1964-2000

paragraphs.text: As the lower ice melted away, the glaciologist Bethan Davies notes, some glaciers were left hanging on steep rock, without the ice that used to hold them from below.
Scientists say warming likely made a collapse like this more probable. They do not say it caused this one on its own.
Most of the people the flood reached were nowhere near the ice. Many were at work, some of them inside the mountain.
These two rivers are some of Nepal's most important power lines. Hydropower plants and their tunnels sit all along the Bhotekoshi and the Trishuli.
Twelve hydropower projects were damaged. About 430 megawatts went offline, roughly a tenth of the country's hydro and solar output.

stat.label: Offline after the flood, about 10.6 % of Nepal's hydro and solar output
stat.source: Ministry of Energy, via Kathmandu Post, Oct 6, 2026

paragraphs.text: Many of these plants send the river through tunnels cut into the rock. When the flood came, people were working inside them.
In the first weeks, officials said more than nine hundred people at these projects were missing, some of them believed trapped underground.

stat.label: Missing at 12 hydropower projects, first weeks

paragraphs.text: On September 17, the disaster authority reported that teams had dug through 250 metres of tunnel at the Chilime plant and found five bodies. At Upper Trishuli-1, five more were still trapped, waiting for cutting equipment.

document.text: Five bodies were recovered after teams broke through the 250-metre tunnel and cleared access to the control room.
At Upper Trishuli-1, five bodies remain trapped inside the tunnel, with recovery pending the availability of cutting equipment.

paragraphs.text: On August 31, the army set off a controlled blast inside a tunnel at Upper Trishuli 3A to reach the workers missing there.
There were survivors. On September 4, nine days after the flood, two hydropower workers came out alive after nine days trapped underground. The next day rescuers found two more people alive.
Projects still under construction were hit as well, about 3,800 megawatts of planned capacity.

stat.label: Planned capacity at hit projects under construction
stat.source: Ministry of Energy, via Kathmandu Post, 2026

paragraphs.text: Some of these plants had only just been repaired after the 2025 flood.
Nepal sells electricity to India and counts on its rivers to grow. Should it keep building in valleys like this one?

ask.text: Keep building dams in these valleys?

paragraphs.text: By October 5, Nepal counted 1,455 dead and 5,285 missing. The number of dead had kept climbing for six weeks.

chart.title: Confirmed dead in Nepal
chart.source: NDRRMA via Himalayan Times; Kathmandu Post; Reuters

paragraphs.text: Missing does not always mean dead. Officials say the lists include unidentified bodies and people who have since been found.
Search and rescue ended on October 5, with more than 13,000 people rescued. Then came identification. By the end of September, DNA had been taken from 1,334 bodies to put names to them.

stat.label: People rescued by the end of search and rescue, 5 October
Bodies sampled for DNA by 30 September

paragraphs.text: UNICEF counted about 84,000 people affected, 32,000 of them children. 102 children were orphaned.

stat.label: People affected, 32,021 of them children

paragraphs.text: In September the disaster authority counted 636 foreign nationals among the missing: trekkers, pilgrims and workers.

stat.label: Foreign nationals among the missing, 20 September

paragraphs.text: Nepal's law made families wait twelve years before a missing person could be declared dead. In October the cabinet proposed cutting that to forty-five days.

stat.label: Before a missing person can be declared dead (proposed)

paragraphs.text: On the Chinese side the official figures were 43 dead and 519 missing by mid-September. Videos and eyewitness posts from Tibet were removed from Chinese social media, according to the BBC and the New York Times, and police punished at least ten people for what they called misleading posts.

stat.label: Tibet, official figures, mid-September

paragraphs.text: At first Nepal turned down rescue teams from several countries, saying its own forces could handle the operation. Under diplomatic pressure it later let in experts from India, China, Australia and South Korea.
Aid came from India, China, the United States, Australia, the Gulf states and others. The Loss and Damage Fund, set up for climate disasters, gave twenty million dollars.

stat.label: From the Loss and Damage Fund

paragraphs.text: In Nepal, the first rumours blamed a Chinese dam. The satellite images showed the mountain itself.
The government counts 7,570 houses destroyed and puts reconstruction at about 4.8 billion dollars, for a country whose whole economy is around forty billion.

stat.label: To rebuild, by the government's assessment
stat.source: Government of Nepal, Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment, 2026

paragraphs.text: Langtang is one valley. How many more look like it?
In February 2021, a rock and ice avalanche in Chamoli, India, sent a flood through two hydropower projects.
In October 2023, a glacial lake in Sikkim burst and destroyed the 1,200 megawatt Teesta III dam.

shots.on_screen_text: South Lhonak and the Teesta, Sikkim

paragraphs.text: A year and a half later, the government approved rebuilding it.

shots.on_screen_text: Glaciers on the Tibetan side of the Himalaya, ISS, May 2026

paragraphs.text: In August 2024, floods from glacial lakes wiped out much of Thame, a village near Everest. It came in daylight, and no one died.

shots.on_screen_text: The Himalaya between Nepal and Tibet, ISS, May 2026

paragraphs.text: ICIMOD counts five significant glacial lake floods in the Everest region in less than fifty years.

stat.label: Major glacial lake floods near Everest in under 50 years

paragraphs.text: In July 2025, Rasuwagadhi. In August 2026, Rasuwagadhi again, and worse than all of them together.

In 2023, ICIMOD projected that the region's glaciers could lose thirty to fifty percent of their volume by 2100, even if warming is held to one and a half or two degrees. At three degrees, glaciers in the eastern Himalaya, which includes Nepal, could lose up to three quarters.

stat.label: Glacier volume the region could lose by 2100 at 1.5-2 °C

shots.photo: File:Snow-capped Mountains at Kyanjin Gompa Rasuwa.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Glaciers on the Tibetan side of the Himalaya, ISS, May 2026

stat.label: Eastern Himalaya glacier volume lost by 2100 at 3 °C

paragraphs.text: The same report found that the region's glaciers lost mass sixty-five percent faster in the 2010s than in the decade before.

stat.label: Faster glacier loss in 2011-2020 than in the decade before

paragraphs.text: Shrinking ice does not mean every glacier will fall. But it leaves more ice hanging on steeper rock, and more lakes behind loose walls, above valleys where people live and work.

shots.on_screen_text: Glaciers on the Tibetan side of the Himalaya, ISS, May 2026

paragraphs.text: Nepal says it will rebuild its warning system on the border with China. In September its disaster authority and ICIMOD published a list of ten points for action.

shots.on_screen_text: The Himalaya between Nepal and Tibet, ISS, May 2026

paragraphs.text: This flood showed the hard part. The danger started on one side of a border and above every station, and it moved faster than an alert could travel. Yet the glacier's movement was visible from space before it fell.
We will keep following these valleys from orbit. So who should watch the ice above a river that two countries share, and who should have the power to pull the alarm?

shots.on_screen_text: Glaciers on the Tibetan side of the Himalaya, ISS, May 2026

youtube.title: Nepal's Flood Warning Came 38 Minutes Too Late
youtube.description: On 26 August 2026 a block of ice and rock broke off Langtang Lirung, on Nepal's border with Tibet, and became a flood that ran about 100 km down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. We follow it from orbit with Sentinel-2 and Landsat images: the scar on the mountain, the border crossing at Rasuwagadhi, the 38 minutes before the text alerts, the same valley's disasters in 2015 and 2025, the hydropower tunnels in its path, and what the shrinking glaciers of the Himalaya mean for the next valley.
youtube.pinned_comment: Who should watch the ice above a river two countries share, and who should have the power to pull the alarm?
